name: Mobills
tagline: Brazilian personal finance app for tracking expenses, credit card bills and monthly budgets.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The ledger itself is not hard: accounts, categories, transactions, recurring entries, a monthly budget per category, and a few charts. An agent can produce that in a session and you will own your data instead of renting it. What you will not get in a session is the part that makes a finance app stick: automatic bank and card syncing through Open Finance, a polished phone app you actually open at the checkout counter, and credit card invoice logic that handles closing dates, installments and partial payments the way Brazilians actually spend. Installment purchases alone, the classic 12x parcelado, are a surprising amount of modeling work. Build it if you are willing to type your spending in manually, which is also roughly what most Mobills free users do anyway.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you log transactions against accounts and categories, set monthly budgets, and see where the month went.
requirements: Somewhere to run it, a laptop or a cheap VPS
Willingness to enter transactions by hand
whatYouLose: Automatic bank and credit card sync via Open Finance
Native iOS and Android apps with widgets and offline entry
Solid credit card invoice handling: closing dates, installments, partial payments
Backups and sync across devices that someone else maintains
moatNotes: The real work is bank connectivity under Brazilian Open Finance rules, which is not something you bolt on over a weekend.
whyPeopleStillPay: A finance tracker only works if logging is frictionless, and frictionless means a native app in your pocket plus transactions that show up without you typing them. People pay for the sync and the habit, not the spreadsheet math. The moment you have to open a laptop to record a coffee, the ledger goes stale and the whole thing is worthless.
notes: Great build if you like your money data local, assuming you are the kind of person who actually logs things.
prompt:
Build a single-user personal finance tracker that runs locally. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router, TypeScript)
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/finance.db
- Tailwind CSS for styling
- Recharts for charts
- Zod for input validation

Data model:
- accounts: id, name, type (checking, savings, cash, credit_card), opening_balance, closing_day and due_day for credit cards
- categories: id, name, kind (income or expense), color
- transactions: id, date, description, amount in integer cents, kind (income, expense, transfer), account_id, category_id, notes
- installments: a purchase can create N linked transactions, one per month, tagged with a shared purchase_id and "3/12" style labels
- budgets: month (YYYY-MM), category_id, limit in cents

Features that must work:
- Add, edit and delete transactions fast. Keyboard-first form: date, amount, category, account, description.
- Month view: total income, total expense, net, and a per-category breakdown table.
- Budget page: set a monthly limit per category, show spent vs limit with a progress bar, highlight overruns in red.
- Credit card page: group a card's transactions into invoices by closing day, show the current open invoice total and the next due date.
- Installment purchases: enter total amount and number of months, the app generates the linked monthly transactions.
- Charts: expense by category (pie) and net by month for the last 12 months (bar).
- CSV import with a column mapping step, and CSV export of all transactions.
- Mobile layout that is genuinely usable, plus a web manifest so it installs as a PWA.

Out of scope, do not attempt: bank or Open Finance integration, multi-user, authentication, receipt OCR, push notifications, investment tracking.

Seed the database with a handful of example categories and two accounts. Store currency and locale in .env (default BRL, pt-BR) and format all money with Intl.NumberFormat. Amounts are integer cents everywhere, never floats. Include a README with setup, a backup note (copy the .db file), and a one-command dev start.
